case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a voluntary departure deadline under immigration law is extended to the next business day when the final day of the departure period falls on a weekend or legal holiday.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1229c (Immigration and Nationality Act's voluntary departure provisions), along with related BIA regulations and procedural rules governing voluntary departure deadlines in removal proceedings.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hugo Monsalvo Velázquez argues that the longstanding common-law rule — which extends deadlines falling on weekends or legal holidays to the next business day — should apply to voluntary departure periods, consistent with the Ninth Circuit's approach in Meza-Vallejos. He contends that his 60-day voluntary departure period ended on a weekend, making his Monday filing timely. He further argues that the BIA's own Practice Manual acknowledges this extension principle for filing deadlines, that the Tenth Circuit's contrary rule creates unintended practical hardships Congress never contemplated, and that the rule of immigration lenity requires resolving any ambiguity in the statute in the noncitizen's favor.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government (Attorney General Garland), as upheld by the Tenth Circuit and the BIA, argues that voluntary departure deadlines are substantive departure requirements — not merely procedural filing deadlines — and therefore the common-law next-business-day extension rule does not apply. The BIA reasoned that its Practice Manual provisions extending deadlines apply only to the filing of appeals and motions with immigration courts or the Board, not to the voluntary departure period itself, meaning Monsalvo's departure or motion to reopen filed after the 60-day calendar period was untimely regardless of the weekend.
key_precedents: Meza-Vallejos v. Holder (Ninth Circuit) — held that voluntary departure deadlines falling on weekends are extended to the next business day
Salvador-Calleros (circuit court decision cited as part of the circuit split)
Barroso (circuit court decision cited as part of the circuit split)
Niz-Chavez v. Garland (2021) — cited by Monsalvo in his motion to reopen as a change in law regarding notice to appear
Avery v. Stewart, 2 Conn. 69 (1816) — early common-law precedent establishing the Sunday/holiday deadline extension rule for contractual obligations
Salter v. Burt, 20 Wend. 205 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1838) — supporting common-law deadline extension rule
Hammond v. Am. Mut. Life Ins. Co., 10 Gray 306 (Mass. 1858) — supporting common-law deadline extension rule
Sherwood Bros. v. District of Columbia, 113 F.2d 162 (D.C. Cir.) — recognizing the common-law deadline rule as embedded in community custom
Barnes v. [Rhode Island case], 12 R.I. 26 — synthesizing the common-law rule on Sunday deadline extensions
U.S. Constitution, Art. I, §7, cl. 2 (Presentment Clause) — cited for the constitutional recognition of Sunday as a dies non

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and I find my confidence strengthened rather than diminished by the quality of the deliberation. Justice Alito's movement to the Petitioner side — despite his initial skepticism — is particularly significant, as he is the colleague most likely to identify weaknesses in the common-law incorporation argument, and his acknowledgment that 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) substantially undermines the government's procedural/substantive distinction confirms that this regulatory backdrop is the strongest and narrowest ground for decision. As I noted in my prior reasoning, Justice Jackson's point about §1.1(h) remains the most defensible basis for the majority opinion: we need not broadly restructure voluntary departure law or endorse expansive lenity principles if we can resolve this case on the narrow ground that Congress enacted §1229c against a regulatory backdrop that already incorporated the weekend-and-holiday extension, and nothing in the statutory text affirmatively displaces that established meaning. As Chief Justice, I will assign the majority opinion with instructions to hold narrowly on the §1.1(h) regulatory backdrop combined with the Astoria Federal presumption, explicitly reserving broader questions about the scope of the dies non rule in immigration enforcement contexts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito's movement toward the Petitioner position, despite his initial skepticism, is particularly significant from an originalist standpoint — his concession that the government's procedural/substantive distinction 'lacks the textual grounding necessary to overcome this presumption' confirms that even a justice skeptical of broad common-law incorporation cannot find affirmative displacement in §1229c's text. Justice Jackson's point about 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) remains the strongest textual anchor under my methodology: Congress enacted the INA against a regulatory backdrop that already embedded the weekend-and-holiday extension principle, and the original public meaning of '60 days' in §1229c must be understood in light of that preexisting legal context. The historical cases — Avery v. Stewart and Hammond v. American Mutual Life Insurance Co. — directly refute the government's categorical distinction between procedural filings and substantive performance obligations, demonstrating that the dies non rule was part of the background common law Congress inherited in 1952. Under Astoria Federal's presumption that Congress legislates against settled common-law backdrops, and absent any affirmative textual signal displacing the extension principle, the Petitioner's position is compelled by the original public meaning of the statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: After careful deliberation, I find that the convergence of Justice Barrett's textualist argument about 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) and Justice Thomas's originalist point about the common-law backdrop Congress inherited in 1952 has substantially resolved my earlier skepticism. The government's procedural/substantive distinction — which was my primary remaining concern — lacks the historical grounding necessary to overcome the presumption from Astoria Federal that Congress legislates against settled common-law backdrops, particularly when the agency's own preexisting regulatory framework had already incorporated the weekend-and-holiday extension principle. I remain somewhat cautious about the breadth of this ruling and would join Chief Justice Roberts in confining the holding to the narrowest available ground: that §1229c(b)(2)'s '60 days' must be read against the regulatory backdrop of §1.1(h) and the common-law dies non principle, without broadly restructuring voluntary departure law or endorsing expansive immigration lenity principles that could unsettle enforcement in other contexts. The near-unanimous agreement among colleagues across divergent methodological commitments — while not itself dispositive — does confirm that the government has failed to identify any affirmative textual displacement of a background principle that its own regulatory framework had already embedded.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious challenge — that the dies non rule was historically confined to procedural court filings, not substantive performance obligations — but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, Avery v. Stewart and Hammond v. American Mutual Life Insurance Co. directly refute this characterization by applying the rule to contractual yarn-delivery and insurance payment obligations, which are quintessentially substantive performance acts. Justice Jackson's point about 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) is particularly powerful and reinforces my position: the preexisting immigration regulation explicitly incorporating the weekend-and-holiday extension rule into the computation of 'day' strongly suggests Congress understood '60 days' in §1229c to carry this same conventional legal meaning. Justice Alito's concern about uncertainty in removal proceedings has some practical weight, but the far greater uncertainty — and injustice — lies in subjecting noncitizens to permanent ten-year bars based on the fortuity of which day of the week a government-imposed deadline happens to fall, a result that falls hardest on the most vulnerable and least legally sophisticated immigrants. The near-unanimous consensus among my colleagues across very different methodological commitments — originalism, textualism, pragmatism — that the common-law backdrop governs here absent clear congressional displacement gives me additional confidence that this is the correct result.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The near-unanimous convergence across radically different methodological commitments — Justice Thomas's originalism, Justice Gorsuch's textualism, Justice Sotomayor's purposivism — on the same result is itself significant evidence that the legal foundation here is sound, not merely a product of ideological alignment. Justice Jackson's 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) argument remains my strongest anchor as a pragmatic textualist: the preexisting regulatory definition of 'day' in immigration proceedings already embedded the weekend-and-holiday extension, meaning Congress enacted §1229c against a backdrop that treated deadline computation this way, and the government cannot overcome that contextual evidence with an unsupported procedural/substantive distinction. Justice Alito's movement to Petitioner — despite his initial skepticism and his natural inclination toward enforcement-side arguments — is particularly telling, because he is the justice most likely to find merit in the government's position, and his concession that the government's distinction 'lacks the textual grounding necessary to overcome this presumption' confirms that the respondent's best argument has been tested and found wanting. I maintain my position with slightly increased confidence, and would join Chief Justice Roberts's preference for resolving this on the narrow ground of the §1.1(h) regulatory backdrop combined with the Astoria Federal common-law presumption, without broadly restructuring voluntary departure law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the dies non rule was principally developed for court filings and legal proceedings, not affirmative acts in the world, and that the BIA's distinction between filing deadlines and substantive departure requirements reflects a sensible regulatory reading. But this argument fails on the historical record: Avery v. Stewart applied the rule to a contractual yarn-delivery deadline, and Hammond applied it to insurance obligations — neither involved court filings. The government's procedural/substantive distinction is simply not how the common-law rule was originally understood or applied. Justice Jackson's point about 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) is particularly compelling to my originalist methodology: when the very regulatory framework implementing the INA explicitly incorporated the weekend-and-holiday extension rule for computing 'periods of time,' that strongly confirms Congress legislated against a backdrop that included this principle, and nothing in §1229c's text affirmatively displaces it. The rule of lenity in immigration matters, combined with the presumption that Congress legislates against settled common-law backdrops per Astoria Federal, seals the analysis in Monsalvo's favor.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito's movement toward the petitioner's position — driven in significant part by the 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) regulatory backdrop argument — confirms what I identified in round one as the strongest narrow ground for decision. As an institutionalist, I find the regulatory backdrop argument particularly sound because it allows us to resolve this case without broadly restructuring voluntary departure law or endorsing sweeping immigration lenity principles: Congress enacted §1229c against a preexisting regulatory framework that already incorporated the weekend-and-holiday extension, and the government cannot demonstrate affirmative displacement of that background understanding from the statutory text alone. Justice Alito's residual concern about 'uncertainty in removal proceedings' deserves acknowledgment, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, the Tenth Circuit's rigid calendar rule produces its own workability-defeating anomalies — including the arbitrary disparity between noncitizens whose deadlines fall on weekdays versus weekends — that signal a misreading of congressional intent. I maintain my position with slightly increased confidence, and would join a majority opinion written on the narrowest available ground consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's preference for institutional restraint.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito's movement toward the petitioner's position — driven in significant part by the 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) argument I raised — confirms that the regulatory backdrop argument is the strongest and narrowest ground for decision. The government's procedural/substantive distinction, which was the most serious challenge to our position, has now been thoroughly undermined both by the historical record (Avery v. Stewart, Hammond) and by the internal logic of the immigration regulatory framework itself: if the agency's own preexisting regulation defining 'day' for computing time periods incorporated the weekend-and-holiday extension, the government cannot credibly argue that Congress intended §1229c's '60 days' to operate on a different, harsher calendar. Consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's preference for narrow grounds, I would write to resolve this case on the limited proposition that Congress enacted §1229c against a regulatory backdrop — embodied in 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) — that already incorporated the extension principle, and nothing in the statutory text affirmatively displaces that background understanding. The near-unanimous agreement across methodologically diverse colleagues, including Justice Alito's partial conversion, gives me additional confidence that this result is correct, though I would caution against broad pronouncements about immigration lenity that could unsettle adjacent areas of removal law.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the dies non rule was historically confined to court filings and legal proceedings, not affirmative physical acts like departing the country — but as Justices Gorsuch and Sotomayor correctly note, this distinction collapses under historical scrutiny: Avery v. Stewart applied the rule to a contractual yarn-delivery obligation, and Hammond applied it to insurance performance, both involving physical acts rather than court filings. My background as a public defender makes me acutely sensitive to Justice Alito's concern about 'uncertainty in removal proceedings,' but that concern is outweighed by the asymmetric severity of the consequence — a ten-year bar — imposed on noncitizens for missing a deadline by one day due to circumstances entirely outside their control, which is precisely the kind of disproportionate outcome the common-law rule was designed to prevent. The preexisting 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) regulatory definition incorporating the weekend-and-holiday extension for computing 'day' in immigration proceedings remains my strongest textual anchor, as it demonstrates that Congress legislated §1229c against a regulatory backdrop that already embedded this principle. I maintain my position with slightly increased confidence given the near-unanimous agreement among colleagues and the failure of the government's procedural/substantive distinction to find support in either the statutory text or the historical record.

John Roberts.reasoning: The common-law dies non juridicus rule represents a deeply embedded background principle that federal courts have long incorporated into statutory interpretation even absent explicit textual authorization, as recognized in Street v. United States, 133 U.S. 299 (1890), and the Court's broader practice of reading traditional common-law qualifications into federal statutes. While the government's distinction between procedural filing deadlines and substantive departure requirements has some force, the narrow question here is whether Congress, in enacting 8 U.S.C. § 1229c, affirmatively displaced this centuries-old background rule — and the statutory text provides no clear indication that it did. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would resolve this case on the limited ground that the common-law extension principle applies absent explicit congressional displacement, without broadly addressing the rule of lenity or restructuring voluntary departure law more generally. This approach also respects institutional legitimacy by resolving a genuine circuit split — between the Ninth Circuit's Meza-Vallejos and the Tenth Circuit's contrary rule — on the narrowest available grounds rather than leaving noncitizens subject to inconsistent standards depending solely on geography.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist, I find the historical record compelling: the dies non juridicus principle predates the Founding, was firmly embedded in English common law through cases like Careswell v. Vaughan (1668) and Swann v. Broome (1764), and was adopted in early American jurisprudence through Avery v. Stewart (1816) and its progeny as a background principle of general applicability — not confined merely to procedural court filings. The INA's own implementing regulations from 1952 codified this tradition by defining 'day' to exclude Sundays and legal holidays when computing any action period, and the DOJ's own Practice Manual extends this principle to filing deadlines in immigration proceedings, suggesting the agency itself understood the rule broadly. The government's distinction between 'substantive' departure requirements and 'procedural' filing deadlines is not grounded in the statutory text of 8 U.S.C. § 1229c, which is silent on this question, and importing an atextual carve-out that disadvantages noncitizens contradicts the background common-law rule Congress legislated against. While I am skeptical of immigration lenity as a freestanding canon, the original public meaning of deadline computation rules, combined with the regulatory history, supports extending the departure period to the next business day.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I am skeptical of importing common-law background principles into statutory schemes where Congress has established a specific, detailed regulatory framework governing voluntary departure. The voluntary departure period under 8 U.S.C. § 1229c is a substantive departure requirement — an affirmative obligation to physically leave the country — not a procedural filing deadline, and the historical dies non rule, as illustrated by cases like Avery v. Stewart and Hammond v. American Mutual Life Insurance Co., was principally developed to address court filings and legal proceedings on non-juridical days, not to extend the time for performing affirmative acts in the world. The BIA's reasonable distinction between filing deadlines (covered by its Practice Manual) and the voluntary departure period itself reflects a sensible reading of the regulatory structure, and courts should defer to that agency interpretation rather than expansively applying a common-law gloss that Congress never incorporated into the INA's text. Furthermore, the practical consequences of extending voluntary departure deadlines cut against petitioner: such extensions create uncertainty in removal proceedings and undermine the government's legitimate interest in enforcing orderly departure requirements, concerns that weigh heavily in my analysis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The centuries-old common-law dies non juridicus principle — recognized by this Court in Street v. United States and embedded in American legal tradition since before the Founding — should apply to voluntary departure deadlines absent a clear congressional directive to the contrary. The government's distinction between 'procedural filing deadlines' and 'substantive performance deadlines' is formalistic and unsupported by the historical record; common-law courts applied the next-business-day extension to contractual performance obligations, not merely court filings, as demonstrated by Avery v. Stewart and Hammond v. American Mutual Life Insurance Co. The practical consequences of the Tenth Circuit's rigid rule fall hardest on vulnerable noncitizens who, through no fault of their own, face the permanent penalty of a ten-year bar on adjustment of status simply because a government-imposed deadline happened to expire on a Sunday — a result Congress never contemplated and one that the rule of immigration lenity requires us to resolve in Monsalvo's favor. Furthermore, the BIA's own Practice Manual acknowledges deadline extension principles, undermining the government's claim that voluntary departure periods occupy a categorically different legal space.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The common-law dies non rule — extending deadlines falling on weekends or legal holidays to the next business day — is so deeply embedded in our legal tradition that Congress is presumed to legislate against its backdrop, and nothing in 8 U.S.C. § 1229c's text affirmatively displaces it. The government's procedural/substantive distinction is not a principled legal boundary with historical pedigree; rather, as the research confirms, courts applying the common-law rule from Avery v. Stewart through modern practice have never consistently drawn that line, and the BIA's own Practice Manual implicitly acknowledges the extension principle for immigration deadlines. Refusing to apply the rule here creates the kind of arbitrary, workability-defeating anomaly I find most troubling: noncitizens with e-filing access effectively receive a longer departure period than those without it, conditioning a statutory right on the fortuity of technological access and government infrastructure choices rather than on anything Congress contemplated. The Ninth Circuit's approach in Meza-Vallejos better honors statutory coherence, avoids a needless trap for noncitizens acting in good faith, and aligns with the broader principle that courts read federal statutes to incorporate traditional common-law qualifications absent clear contrary congressional intent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The historical record is clear: the common-law dies non rule was never confined to procedural filing deadlines but applied broadly to substantive performance obligations, as demonstrated by Avery v. Stewart's application to a contractual yarn-delivery deadline and Hammond v. American Mutual Life Insurance Co.'s application to insurance obligations — both involving physical acts of performance, not mere court filings. As an originalist and textualist, I must ask what background legal principles Congress legislated against when it enacted the voluntary departure provisions of 8 U.S.C. § 1229c, and the answer is unmistakable: the common-law rule extending deadlines falling on Sundays and holidays to the next business day was, by the twentieth century, 'embedded in the habits and customs of the community' per Sherwood Bros., applying to substantive acts as readily as procedural ones. The government's distinction between 'substantive departure requirements' and 'procedural filing deadlines' finds no support in the original common-law rule's scope, and where Congress legislates against a backdrop of settled common law without displacing it, we presume that backdrop governs; moreover, the rule of lenity in immigration matters counsels resolving any remaining ambiguity in Monsalvo's favor.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The longstanding common-law dies non juridicus principle, recognized by this Court in Street v. United States and embedded in American legal tradition since before the Founding, strongly supports extending voluntary departure deadlines that fall on weekends or holidays to the next business day. As an institutionalist who values history and tradition, I find it significant that this background principle has been consistently incorporated into federal statutory interpretation even absent explicit textual authorization, and the Court routinely reads federal statutes to incorporate such traditional common-law qualifications. The government's distinction between 'procedural filing deadlines' and 'substantive departure requirements' is not persuasive given that the practical effect of the deadline — requiring action on a day when courts and government offices are closed — creates the same impossibility the common-law rule was designed to remedy. Furthermore, the near-universal practice of the immigration bar, immigration judges, and federal circuits outside the Tenth Circuit reflects a settled understanding that workability and practical administration of the voluntary departure system require this extension, consistent with my emphasis on practical workability as a key decision factor.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must ask what background principles Congress legislated against when it enacted 8 U.S.C. §1229c(b)(2). The historical record is compelling: the common-law dies non rule extending deadlines falling on Sundays and holidays to the next business day was well-established across American jurisprudence by the 19th century, applied not merely to procedural filings but to substantive contractual performance obligations as illustrated in Avery v. Stewart, Salter v. Burt, and Hammond v. American Mutual Life Insurance Co. Under Astoria Federal Savings & Loan Ass'n v. Solimino, Congress is presumed to legislate with awareness of well-established common-law adjudicatory principles, and nothing in §1229c's text affirmatively displaces this centuries-old background rule. The government's distinction between 'procedural filing deadlines' and 'substantive departure requirements' is textually unmoored — the statute simply specifies a period of days, and the common-law rule for computing such periods when they expire on a dies non applies with equal force absent clear congressional intent to the contrary.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The common-law rule extending deadlines falling on weekends and legal holidays to the next business day is a deeply embedded legal principle with roots stretching back to Avery v. Stewart (1816) and recognized across federal jurisprudence, and Congress is presumed to legislate against this backdrop unless it expressly negates such principles, as established in Lexmark. The statutory text of 8 U.S.C. §1229c(b)(2) — providing that voluntary departure 'shall not be valid for a period exceeding 60 days' — contains no clear indication that Congress intended to displace this common-law rule, and the government's characterization of the deadline as 'substantive' rather than 'procedural' does not resolve the interpretive question, because the petitioner is not seeking an equitable extension but rather the best ordinary reading of what '60 days' means under established legal conventions. Critically, 8 C.F.R. §1.1(h) (1996), the preexisting immigration regulation defining 'day' for computing periods of time, explicitly incorporates the weekend-and-holiday extension rule, strongly suggesting that Congress understood '60 days' in §1229c to carry this same meaning. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that the Tenth Circuit's rigid calendar rule imposes severe, disproportionate consequences — permanent bars on relief — on noncitizens for missing a deadline by a single day due to circumstances entirely outside their control, a result Congress almost certainly never contemplated.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito's shift is significant — his concession that the 1952 implementing regulations defined 'day' to exclude Sundays and holidays for computing 'any action period' under the INA is precisely the kind of contemporaneous regulatory evidence that confirms the common-law backdrop canon applies here. With a unanimous conference, my task as Chief Justice is to ensure the majority opinion is written narrowly enough to command genuine agreement rather than producing a fractured ruling with multiple concurrences that dilutes the holding's precedential force. I will assign the opinion with instructions to ground the holding specifically in the common-law dies non backdrop against which Congress enacted § 1229c and the 1952 regulatory confirmation of that backdrop, while expressly declining to rest on the immigration rule of lenity as an independent rationale — consistent with my earlier reasoning and Justice Kavanaugh's agreement on that point. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson may wish to write separately to address the rule of lenity and equity concerns, which I would not foreclose but would keep out of the majority opinion to preserve the narrowest possible grounds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious challenge to our position — that the dies non rule developed in the context of court filings and appearances, not substantive conditions of relief — but this distinction finds no support in the historical record. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, 19th-century courts applied the extension rule to contractual performance obligations and other substantive deadlines without drawing any categorical line between 'procedural' and 'substantive' duties. The original public meaning inquiry is dispositive here: when Congress enacted 8 U.S.C. § 1229c against the backdrop of a well-established common-law principle that courts had applied universally to all legal deadlines, its silence on displacing that principle must be read as incorporation, not abrogation — precisely the interpretive canon I applied in Wyeth v. Levine and that textualism demands. Justice Gorsuch's invocation of the Presentment Clause's treatment of Sundays as non-juridical days further confirms that the Founders themselves understood this principle to operate broadly across legal contexts, not merely in the narrow procedural filing context the government now urges.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas's point about the 1952 INA implementing regulations defining 'day' to exclude Sundays and legal holidays for 'taking any action' under the statute remains the most compelling datum for me — it represents contemporaneous administrative construction of the very statute at issue, and under my textualist methodology, that original regulatory understanding carries significant weight in establishing the background against which Congress legislated. Justice Barrett's observation that departure practically requires coordination with immigration authorities and presentation at ports of entry — all of which implicate the same closure concerns animating the dies non rule — partially addresses my residual concern that physical departure differs categorically from a court filing, though I remain less than fully persuaded that the analogy is perfect. My principal remaining reservation is that the dies non tradition developed in contexts where legal compulsion was suspended on non-juridical days, whereas a noncitizen can physically depart on a Sunday regardless of office closures; however, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, the 1952 regulatory evidence and the absence of any express congressional abrogation of the background principle together overcome that reservation. I therefore maintain my vote for Petitioner while continuing to favor Chief Justice Roberts's narrow formulation limiting the holding to circumstances where departure-related government offices are closed or unavailable on the final day of the period.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the dies non rule developed in the context of court filings and appearances, not substantive conditions of relief like physical departure from the country. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson both demonstrate through careful historical analysis, the common-law rule was never so narrowly cabined: 19th-century courts applied it to contractual performance obligations and other substantive deadlines, not merely procedural filings. The government's 'substantive vs. procedural' distinction is a modern invention without historical grounding, and the practical consequences of accepting it are deeply troubling from my perspective — noncitizens without access to e-filing or counsel face a shorter effective departure window through no fault of their own, a result that harms the most vulnerable immigrant populations and that Congress never contemplated when enacting § 1229c. The combination of the deeply embedded common-law backdrop, the BIA's own recognition of the principle in Matter of Escobar, the immigration rule of lenity from INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, and the arbitrary real-world disparities the government's rule creates all reinforce my conviction that the petitioner must prevail.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious challenge — that the dies non rule developed in the context of court filings and appearances, not substantive conditions of relief, and that the voluntary departure period is categorically different because it requires a physical act (leaving the country) rather than a filing. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson both note, the historical record simply does not support that categorical distinction: 19th-century courts applied the Sunday extension rule to contractual performance obligations and other substantive deadlines, not merely procedural filings. The government's 'substantive vs. procedural' line also collapses under structural analysis — the practical effect on the noncitizen is identical whether the deadline is characterized as substantive or procedural, and as I noted in my initial reasoning, the BIA's own Practice Manual extends the next-business-day rule to immigration court filings while denying it to the underlying departure period, creating an incoherent scheme that no sensible reading of the statute demands. The canon that Congress legislates against deeply embedded common-law background principles, combined with the immigration rule of lenity for any residual ambiguity, firmly supports the petitioner's position.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious challenge — that the dies non rule developed in the context of court filings and appearances, not substantive conditions of relief like physical departure from the country. But as Justice Thomas correctly notes, the historical record does not support this procedural/substantive distinction: 19th-century courts applied the Sunday extension rule to contractual performance obligations, which are indistinguishable in character from a voluntary departure period. The key insight is that the common-law rule was never about the nature of the act required, but about the principle that the law does not compel performance on days when legal processes are suspended — and Congress is presumed to legislate against that backdrop absent express abrogation. Justice Alito's reliance on 8 C.F.R. § 1001.1(h) and the BIA Practice Manual actually cuts against his position, as Justice Kagan observes: if the agency itself applies the next-business-day rule to procedural filings in immigration proceedings, it is incoherent to exempt the underlying substantive period from the same background principle that governs the entire statutory scheme.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito's shift is particularly significant — his initial objection that the dies non rule was limited to procedural filings was the strongest argument for the Respondent, and his acknowledgment that the 1952 implementing regulations defined 'day' to exclude Sundays for computing 'any action period' effectively forecloses the substantive/procedural distinction at the textual and historical level. I remain committed to writing narrowly, as Chief Justice Roberts suggests, grounding the holding in the specific common-law backdrop against which Congress enacted § 1229c rather than invoking the immigration rule of lenity as a standalone rationale — the latter risks unintended consequences across the broader statutory scheme that I am not prepared to accept. Justice Barrett's practical observation that departure itself requires coordination with immigration authorities and physical presence at ports of entry reinforces that the closure concerns animating the dies non rule are not merely theoretical here. The unanimous convergence of the Court on this result, including Justice Alito's careful and honest reassessment, gives me confidence that a narrow, historically-grounded holding for Petitioner is both legally sound and institutionally appropriate.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito's shift is particularly significant — his concession that the 1952 implementing regulations defining 'day' to exclude Sundays and legal holidays for computing 'any action period' constitutes strong contemporaneous evidence of the background principle Congress incorporated into § 1229c is precisely the kind of original regulatory context that textualist and originalist methodology demands we take seriously. His remaining reservation about whether physical departure maps cleanly onto the dies non tradition is understandable, but as I noted in my prior reasoning and as Justice Thomas confirms through Street v. United States and the Presentment Clause's treatment of Sundays, the historical record never drew a categorical procedural/substantive line — the principle operated wherever the law imposed a time-bound obligation. Chief Justice Roberts's counsel to write narrowly is well-taken: the holding should be limited to cases where the final day of a voluntary departure period falls on a Sunday or legal holiday when departure-related government processes are unavailable, grounded in the common-law backdrop canon rather than the broader immigration rule of lenity, which I agree could generate unintended consequences across the statutory scheme.
